# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

There's a moment that happens most mornings if I'm paying attention—that peculiar instant when you first wake and haven't yet remembered what day it is or what problems are waiting. The world exists in a kind of neutral suspension. The light is just light. The sounds are just sounds. You haven't yet assembled them into meaning.

I've been thinking lately about how much of life consists of this act of assembly—how we take the raw material of existence and constantly organize it into narratives, problems, significance. And I wonder if we're missing something by doing this so automatically, so completely, that we rarely pause to notice the noticing itself.

There's something almost embarrassing about acknowledging wonder. It feels childish or naive, like you haven't yet learned how the world actually works. We're taught that sophistication means moving beyond amazement, that maturity is recognizing the ordinary as ordinary. But I think we've confused familiarity with understanding. A thing can be familiar and still be extraordinary. A sunset doesn't become less remarkable because it happens every day.

I was in a café yesterday—the kind of aggressively ordinary place that exists in every city, designed to be pleasantly forgettable—and I watched a woman tear open a packet of sugar and pour it into her coffee. Nothing remarkable. Except that I really looked at it. The crystalline granules, each one a tiny solid thing, dissolving into liquid and changing it. The small gesture of care embedded in the action: she wanted her coffee a particular way and did a small thing to make it so.

This is what I mean about noticing. Not the sugar and coffee themselves, but the underlying reality beneath: that we're all constantly engaged in this practice of small transformations, of making our immediate world slightly more suited to us. Of wanting things and doing modest things to get them.

Everyone you see is this entire universe. That line gets repeated so often it's become almost meaningless, but it's still true. The person sitting across from you on the train has as much interior life as you do—same density of memory, same quality of concern about whether people like them, the same strange loop of consciousness folded back on itself. And you'll never really know them. You'll share space with them and then you'll never meet again, and they'll continue existing after you've forgotten them, living their life according to their own logic.

I think about this when I'm annoyed with someone—in traffic, in a conversation, in my own family. Because there's always a moment where I catch myself and realize: this person has a specific reason for what they're doing. Not an excuse, necessarily. A reason. They're not being a traffic obstruction; they're being late to something. They're not being obtuse in the conversation; they're understanding it through their own history. We're all operating from inside such specific, particular frameworks that conflict is almost inevitable.

The question is whether you meet that with contempt or curiosity.

I've noticed I'm much happier when I choose curiosity. Not in a performative way—not the false listening where you're just waiting for your turn to talk. But genuine curiosity, which is actually quite rare. It requires setting aside, temporarily, your own framework and actually trying to see through someone else's lens. It's harder than it sounds. It requires a kind of humility.

There's a phrase I've been turning over: "the privilege of noticing." I can't remember where I encountered it. But it stuck because it suggests that attention is a kind of fortune, a gift you give yourself. And it's not evenly distributed. Poverty and exhaustion and pain all make noticing harder—when you're desperate or in crisis, the world contracts to just the immediate problem. So there's something almost guilty in having enough space in your life to notice things.

But I think that's exactly why we should do it. Not to feel guilty, but to actually exercise that capacity. Because I suspect that the people who are happiest, in a deep way that has nothing to do with circumstances, are the ones who've somehow maintained this ability to really see things. To see their own small life with the kind of attention normally reserved for art or nature.

There's a writer I love who talks about the "unlived life"—all the ways we move through time on autopilot, doing things without really being present to them. You eat a meal without tasting it. You have a conversation while checking your phone. You drive home and can't remember the drive. You reach the end of a day and it's vanished. That's not really living, even though it looks like living from the outside.

What would it mean to actually live those moments? Not all of them—that would be exhausting and probably impossible. But some of them. To actually taste the meal sometimes. To be fully present in a conversation. To notice the specific quality of light on a particular afternoon, knowing you'll never see this exact combination again because time is moving in one direction and we're all carried forward in it.

Maybe this is what people mean by mindfulness, though that word has been so commercialized and drained of meaning. What I mean is simpler: looking at things. Actually looking.

There's a poem where Mary Oliver asks: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" And the answer everyone gives is: something great, something meaningful, something important.

But I'm increasingly convinced the real answer might be simpler. Notice things. Really see them. Meet people with curiosity rather than judgment. Taste your food. Feel the weather. Read something that changes how you think. Sit with the fact that you exist, which is genuinely improbable, and that you're aware that you exist, which is even more so.

Do that, and maybe everything else organizes itself around it. Or maybe it doesn't, and your life is ordinary in every way.

But you'll have actually lived it. You'll have been present for it.

And that seems like something.
